analysis.one_liner: Rewrites bank-failure and bankruptcy rules so derivatives and repo counterparties can immediately terminate contracts and seize collateral.
analysis.headline: Introduced with the chair and ranking member of the House Financial Services Committee among its cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails or a trading partner goes bankrupt, this bill rewrites who gets paid first and how fast. It guarantees that counterparties holding swaps, repurchase agreements, and other financial contracts can terminate them, offset what they owe against what they are owed, and seize collateral right away, without waiting for a bankruptcy court, and it limits the bankruptcy trustee's power to claw back transfers made just before the collapse. It also bans 'walkaway clauses' that let a winning counterparty walk away from what it owes a failed bank, which protects the deposit insurance fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks, derivatives dealers, broker-dealers, and other financial institutions that trade swaps, repos, and related contracts with banks. They would gain enforceable rights to terminate, net, and accelerate contracts immediately upon a counterparty's failure, court orders could not stop them, and pre-failure transfers under master netting agreements could only be clawed back if actually fraudulent.

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees counterparties to qualified financial contracts — swaps, repos, securities contracts, forward and commodity contracts — the right to terminate, liquidate, or accelerate those contracts when a bank goes into receivership or a trading partner enters bankruptcy.

Adds a new bankruptcy-code section making termination, acceleration, offset, and netting rights under master netting agreements exempt from any stay, avoidance, or court order, so a counterparty can act immediately instead of litigating.

Denies the automatic bankruptcy stay to set-offs under swap and netting agreements, and restricts the bankruptcy trustee's power to undo transfers under master netting agreements to transfers that are fraudulent in nature.

Prohibits enforcement of 'walkaway clauses' — provisions letting a nondefaulting party keep its gains while extinguishing what it owes — in contracts with a failed insured depository institution, so counterparties must pay what they owe the failed bank's estate.

Extends the same framework to contracts with uninsured national banks, certain uninsured state member banks, Edge Act corporations, and foreign banks, requiring that their contractual and netting rights be enforceable to substantially the same extent.

analysis.who_pays: The estates of failed banks and their unsecured creditors, who would recover less because pre-failure transfers under netting agreements largely escape clawback and collateral can be seized immediately. The FDIC's deposit insurance fund indirectly bears some of that cost when recoveries shrink, though it gains from the walkaway-clause ban and retains its power to disaffirm contracts.

drawbacks.text: Restricting the bankruptcy trustee's avoidance powers means transfers a troubled institution made to netting counterparties shortly before collapse generally could not be recovered, leaving less for unsecured creditors and, ultimately, the deposit insurance fund that backstops depositors.

The bill exempts collateralization agreements for qualified financial contracts from the contemporaneous-execution requirement that otherwise lets the FDIC invalidate agreements that were not documented at the time collateral was pledged, weakening a tool the agency uses against undocumented side deals.

The new FDIC recordkeeping authority for qualified financial contracts would apply only to institutions already in troubled condition, so detailed contract records would not be required while a bank is still considered healthy.

The cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: the bill tilts insolvency outcomes toward the largest derivatives counterparties, since the estate's remaining assets — which also cover unsecured creditors — shrink whenever collateral walks out the door on day one.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine compromise design. The case for it is real: when a big bank fails, if counterparties must wait in line like ordinary creditors, each of them can fail in turn, so instant termination and netting rights are meant to stop a chain reaction — a lesson drawn from episodes like Long Term Capital Management in 1998. But the bill pays for that stability out of the pockets of unsecured creditors and, through the deposit insurance fund, ultimately taxpayers, because the special counterparties get paid first and clawback is limited to actual fraud. It includes one clearly public-protective piece — the ban on walkaway clauses — alongside a broad expansion of protections for financial institutions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to two subcommittees in November 2001, never got a markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick Toomey introduced the bill on November 1, 2001, joined at introduction by Reps. Leach, Kanjorski, Oxley, LaFalce, and Baker — the leadership of both parties on the House Financial Services Committee.
The bill was referred to the Financial Services Committee and the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
In late November 2001 it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any Senate action, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one changed position: derivatives dealers did not gain the expanded bankruptcy exemptions they sought, and unsecured creditors and the FDIC kept the existing insolvency rules unchanged. The outcome simply preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Creditors and the FDIC kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — the bill was introduced jointly by three Republicans and three Democrats, including the Financial Services Committee's chair and ranking Democrat, and its 11 cosponsors split 8 Republicans and 3 Democrats; no votes were ever taken, so no opposition pattern appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill locks in immediate termination, offset, and collateral-seizure rights for swap counterparties and shields their pre-failure transfers from clawback. Their guaranteed payout comes out of the failed institution's estate, which unsecured creditors and the deposit insurance fund stand behind.

Repos, reverse repos, margin loans, and related credit enhancements are swept into the protected categories, with damages measured at termination and no stay possible. They get paid first in a bankruptcy at the expense of other creditors.

industries.industry: Securities and futures brokers and clearing organizations
industries.note: The bill lets creditors liquidate or accelerate contracts during securities-industry protective proceedings and preserves brokers' unsecured-claim priority after exercising their rights. Their contractual certainty comes ahead of customer and estate recoveries.

As trading counterparties, banks gain the same netting and termination protections as other financial institutions, and foreign and uninsured banks get the framework extended to them. As failing institutions, they lose walkaway clauses — winning counterparties must pay what they owe the estate — and face FDIC recordkeeping rules once in troubled condition.

industries.industry: FDIC and the deposit insurance fund
industries.note: The fund gains from the walkaway-clause ban and retains its power to transfer or disaffirm qualified financial contracts wholesale. But it absorbs the cost when clawbacks are limited to actual fraud and collateral agreements escape the contemporaneous-execution documentation rule.
